sermon:
## Not Ashamed of the Gospel
*The power that does not need defending*

**Text:** Romans 1:1-17 · **Supporting:** Habakkuk 2:4 · Isaiah 52:7 · 1 Corinthians 1:18 · Mark 8:38

Paul writes to a church in the capital of an empire that crucified its founder, and the first thing he says about himself is that he is a slave. A man writing to Rome, the seat of every power on earth, opens by calling himself owned. He does not lead with credentials. He leads with the one to whom he belongs.

**A gospel older than the man who carries it**
Paul calls himself "a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures" (Romans 1:1-2). Notice what he refuses to do. He will not let anyone treat this message as new. It was not invented in a Galilean village or improvised after a crucifixion. It was promised. The God who speaks in Romans is the God who had already spoken — through Habakkuk, who heard the words Paul will quote in a moment; through Isaiah, who saw the runner on the mountains and cried, "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news" (Isaiah 52:7). The good news did not begin with Paul. He is late to it. He is a witness to something that was true before he believed it, and that is the only kind of gospel worth dying for — one that does not depend on the man who announces it.

We get this wrong constantly. We treat the faith as something we are keeping alive, as if the truth were a fragile thing we must protect from the air. Paul has the opposite instinct. He is not protecting the gospel. He is set apart by it, sent under it, carried along by a message that was running through history long before it reached him.

And then he tells you what the promise was about, and he refuses to leave Jesus a vague figure. The gospel concerns God's Son, "who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead" (Romans 1:3-4). Two natures in one breath. Fully a son of David, born into a real bloodline, a real Israel, a real history. And declared the Son of God in power by an empty tomb. The gospel is not an idea Paul has about God. It is a man who lived and died and rose, anchored in a date and a body, and that is the whole reason it can carry the weight of a Tuesday afternoon. A philosophy comforts you. A risen man can save you.

**The power, not the argument about the power**
Then comes the sentence the whole letter stands on. "For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek" (Romans 1:16). Read it slowly. He does not say the gospel points to the power of God. He does not say it describes the power, or unlocks access to the power, or explains where the power can be found. The gospel is the power. The announcement itself does the saving. When the word is spoken — Christ crucified for sinners, raised for their justification — God's own strength is at work in the speaking of it.

This is why Paul is not ashamed. Shame is what we feel when we are carrying something we are not sure can hold up under scrutiny. But Paul knows what he is holding. To the Greeks who prized wisdom and the Romans who prized strength, a crucified Savior looked like weakness and folly. Paul had stood in those rooms. He knew exactly how it sounded. And he says, in effect, let it sound like folly — "the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God" (1 Corinthians 1:18). The cross does not need to be made respectable before it can save. It saves the way it is.

**The righteousness revealed, not achieved**
And here is the engine underneath it all. "For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith'" (Romans 1:17). The whole letter will unfold this one line. In the gospel, God reveals a righteousness — not a standard we are commanded to reach, but a righteousness from God, given, received, that comes by faith from first to last. Paul reaches back to Habakkuk 2:4 to prove it is not new. The prophet, watching an empire of his own bear down on him, was told that the just would live by faith. Not by strength. Not by the chariots. By trust in the God who keeps his word.

I have to confess something here, because the rotation lands on me before it lands on you. I have preached the gospel as if it were the entry fee and my effort were the building. Believe this, and now go perform. As if Christ got me in the door and the rest were up to my will. But Paul will not let me keep that. From faith to faith. The righteousness that opens the Christian life is the same righteousness that carries it to the end. It is Christ's, credited to me, the moment I stop pleading my own case and trust his. We do not begin with grace and graduate to effort. We live by faith — on day one and on the last day and on every ordinary Tuesday in between.

So the question Romans presses into the first paragraph is not whether you are ashamed to be associated with Jesus in a hostile room. That is the small version. The real question is whether you believe the announcement itself carries God's power — or whether you are still, quietly, trying to add your strength to it. Jesus said it plainly: "whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed" (Mark 8:38). The shame runs both directions. We are tempted to improve the message. To make it land better. To give it the dignity we think it lacks. And every time we do, we are saying we trust our additions more than God's announcement.

The gospel itself is the power.

## The Wrath Already Revealed
*The truth we hold down with both hands*

**Text:** Romans 1:18-32 · **Supporting:** Psalm 19:1 · Romans 2:1 · Ephesians 4:19 · John 3:19

We want the wrath of God to be a future event. Something at the end, after the trumpet, when the books are opened. Paul will not let us file it away there. He uses the present tense. It is being revealed. Now. Already. Not held in reserve for a day that has not come, but breaking out into a world that is running from it at this moment.

**Suppression, not ignorance**
"For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (Romans 1:18). Read that word — suppress. It is the language of holding something down by force. You do not suppress what you have never seen. You suppress what keeps surfacing, what will not stay buried, what rises up in you and has to be pushed back down. Paul's charge against the human race is not that we lacked information. It is that we had it, and we held it under.

"For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse" (Romans 1:19-20). The psalmist said the same: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork" (Psalm 19:1). The witness is everywhere. The morning is a sermon. And the human heart, faced with that sermon, does not say I do not understand. It says I will not have it. The deepest problem is not in the mind. It is in the will. "Although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking" (Romans 1:21).

**The exchange, and the handing over**
Then Paul names the mechanism, and he names it three times. "They exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images" (Romans 1:23). "They exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25). The verb keeps returning because the sin keeps returning. Idolatry is not the absence of worship. It is worship redirected. We do not stop bowing. We bow to what we made.

And here is the terrible turn in the passage, the phrase that should make us go quiet. Three times Paul says God "gave them up." "Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity" (Romans 1:24). "God gave them up to dishonorable passions" (Romans 1:26). "God gave them up to a debased mind" (Romans 1:28). The wrath of God, in this passage, is not lightning. It is release. It is God removing his hand and letting a people have exactly what they insisted on wanting. The judgment is the desire, granted. Paul describes elsewhere people who "have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity" (Ephesians 4:19). Here he says it the other way: God gave them up. Both are true at once. We hand ourselves over, and God honors the handing.

That is a more frightening God than the one who throws thunderbolts. The God who says, very well — have it. The chains you chose. The appetites you fed. The life with me edited out of it.

And we must not read this passage as ancient history, a description of pagan temples and old idolatries that have nothing to do with us. The mechanism is permanent. We still exchange. We still take the glory that belongs to God and pour it onto something he made — a marriage, a child, a reputation, a body, a nation — and then we worship it, and it crushes us, because nothing in creation was built to bear the weight of worship. James K. A. Smith has spent his work arguing that human beings are not first thinkers but lovers, that we are shaped less by what we believe than by what we adore. Romans 1 is the dark side of that truth. We are worshipers by design, and when worship is bent off its true object it does not stop; it spills onto the nearest thing and turns it into a god that devours. The idol always promises freedom and delivers a leash.

**The trap Paul has set for us**
And then, just as the list of sins reaches its full ugliness and we feel the satisfaction of agreeing — yes, that is the world, that is them — Paul turns the whole thing around in the next breath. "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things" (Romans 2:1). The trap was built for the reader who nodded along. He let us climb up onto the seat of judgment for thirty verses, and then he kicked the seat out.

I have to stand in this, because the rotation has come for me too. I have read this chapter from the pulpit with a quiet contempt for the world out there, the debased and the dishonorable, and felt clean by comparison. That contempt is the lie. The suppression Paul describes is not a foreign country. It is the thing I do every time I know the right and choose the lie because the lie is easier, every time I see the glory of God in a thing he made and worship the thing instead. Jesus diagnosed it with one sentence: "the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil" (John 3:19). Loved the darkness. Not stumbled into it. Loved it. That is the human heart, and it is mine.

This is why the gospel had to come the way it came. Not as information for the ignorant — we are not ignorant. As rescue for the guilty who knew, and suppressed, and stand without excuse, and need a righteousness we could never produce because we spent our strength holding the truth down.

We knew, and we suppressed it.

## Every Mouth Stopped
*The verdict no defendant escapes*

**Text:** Romans 2:1-3:20 · **Supporting:** Psalm 14:1-3 · Deuteronomy 10:17 · Romans 3:23 · Galatians 2:16

A courtroom only works if the defendants stop talking. As long as everyone is still explaining, still pointing across the aisle, still entering their qualifications, no verdict can be heard. Paul spends two chapters doing one thing. He is shutting mouths. He moves down the room closing them one by one until the silence is total and the judge can finally speak.

**The judge who shares the crime**
He starts with the moralist — the one who read chapter one and approved. "You have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things" (Romans 2:1). The act of judging is the confession. You could not name the sin if you did not know the sin, and you would not know it so well if it were not your own. Paul presses harder: "Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God?" (Romans 2:3). The most religious man in the room has just been told that his religion is his indictment.

And Paul plants the principle that levels everyone. "For God shows no partiality" (Romans 2:11). It echoes Moses: "For the Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). No bribe. Not your law-keeping, not your heritage, not your decency. God will not be flattered into looking away.

**Having the law is not keeping the law**
Then Paul turns to the man who was sure he was safe — the one who had the Scriptures, the covenant, the circumcision, the name. "For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified" (Romans 2:13). Possession is not performance. To hold the standard is not to meet it. A man can carry the law his whole life and be condemned by the very thing he carried, because the law he owns is the law he broke.

"You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law" (Romans 2:23). The advantage became the accusation. Paul grants every privilege — "the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God" (Romans 3:2), and that is a real and great thing — and then shows that the privilege only deepens the guilt of the one who had the light and lived against it. There is no seat in this courtroom that the light does not reach.

And Paul will not even let the irreligious man relax, the one with no law at all. "For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires... They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness" (Romans 2:14-15). The man without the Bible still has the law carved inside him — a conscience that accuses, an inner court that convenes whether he wants it or not. So there is no escape by ignorance and no escape by privilege. The pagan has the law on his heart and breaks it. The religious man has the law in his hands and breaks it. Different copies of the same standard, the same verdict on both. The most decent person you know and the most degraded person you can imagine are standing on the identical floor, and the floor is sinking.

**No one — and that means you**
Then Paul stops arguing and starts quoting, stacking Scripture on Scripture until there is nowhere left to stand. "None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one" (Romans 3:10-12). He is reading the Psalms back to a people who memorized them: "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.' They are corrupt... there is none who does good" (Psalm 14:1-3). Throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, eyes — he indicts the whole body, the entire instrument of the person, every part of us turned to the wrong use.

And then the gavel. "Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin" (Romans 3:19-20). That is the verdict the whole long argument was driving toward. The law was never a ladder. It was a mirror. It came not to make us righteous but to show us we are not, to close the last open mouth in the room, to leave the whole world standing accountable and silent before God.

I cannot preach this from above it. The mouth Paul is stopping is mine. I have spent years building a quiet case for myself — the ministry done, the sins avoided, the comparisons that always seem to favor me — and Paul takes the brief out of my hands and tears it up. "By works of the law no human being will be justified." No human being. The pastor included. The honest answer to "how are you with God" is never my record, because my record cannot survive the standard. Paul says it flat in Galatians: "by works of the law no one will be justified" (Galatians 2:16). The same sentence. He could not stop saying it.

But a stopped mouth is not the end. It is the beginning. Because the next word in Romans, after every mouth is shut, after every defense collapses, after the courtroom goes silent — the next word is "But." The silence is what makes the But audible. Until you have nothing to say for yourself, you cannot hear what God has to say for you.

No one is righteous, not one.

## But Now a Righteousness From God
*How God stays just and saves the guilty*

**Text:** Romans 3:21-31 · **Supporting:** Leviticus 16:15-16 · Isaiah 53:5 · 2 Corinthians 5:21 · Romans 5:1

Every mouth has been stopped. The whole world stands silent and accountable. And into that silence Paul says one word that the whole letter has been holding its breath to reach. "But now." Two words, and the hinge of the universe turns on them. Everything before was diagnosis. Everything after is gift.

**Apart from the law, and yet witnessed by it**
"But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it — the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe" (Romans 3:21-22). Apart from the law. This is the heart of it. The righteousness that saves does not come up out of our obedience. It comes down, from God, given. The very law that stopped our mouths could never be the source of our standing. And yet — apart from it, but not against it — the Law and the Prophets had been pointing here the whole time, the sacrificial system rehearsing it century after century, Isaiah seeing it from far off: "he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities... and with his wounds we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5).

Paul plants the floor everyone stands on. "For there is no distinction: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:22-23). No distinction. The moralist and the pagan, the churchgoer and the prodigal, the pastor and the man he was tempted to pity — all on the same floor, all short of the same glory. The bad news has to be universal before the good news can be free.

**Justified freely — and a real word for it**
"And are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (Romans 3:24). Justified — declared righteous, the verdict reversed, the accused acquitted not because he was found innocent but because another bore the sentence. By his grace. As a gift. Freely. Paul piles up the words of pure unearned giving because he knows our reflex is to slip our effort back in somewhere.

And then the word the whole passage turns on. God "put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith" (Romans 3:25). Propitiation. We flinch at it, but we must not lose it, because it is the load-bearing word. It means the wrath of chapter one — the wrath already revealed, the God who gives sinners up — that wrath was satisfied. Absorbed. Spent. Not waved away, not pretended out of existence, but borne. The blood of Christ did what the blood of bulls and goats only pictured. On the Day of Atonement the priest took the blood "and sprinkle it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat... because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel" (Leviticus 16:15-16). A covering. A picture, year after year, of a sentence falling somewhere else than on the sinner. And at the cross the picture became the thing. The mercy seat was a man.

**Just, and the justifier**
Now comes the sentence that holds the deepest problem in all of theology and answers it in a single line. God did this "to show his righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:25-26).

Here is the problem Paul has been circling since chapter one. A just judge cannot acquit the guilty. If God simply forgives — overlooks, dismisses, lets it slide — he is not righteous; he is corrupt, a judge who takes the bribe Moses said he would never take. We know this in every other court. A judge who let a murderer walk because he felt warmly toward him would not be merciful; he would be a disgrace to the bench, and the victims would cry out against him. Love that ignores justice is not love; it is indifference wearing love's coat. But if God only condemns, the whole human race is lost, every mouth stopped forever, and the God who is love has no way to reach the people he made. So how does the Holy God forgive sinners without ceasing to be holy? How does he clear the guilty and stay the judge of all the earth?

The cross. At the cross God is both at once. Just — because the sin was punished, fully, in the body of his Son; the law's sentence fell with its full weight. And the justifier — because the one who bore it was God himself in the flesh, so that the guilty go free. Paul says it from another angle: "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). The great exchange. My sin reckoned to him, his righteousness reckoned to me. He took my verdict; I receive his standing.

I have tried for years to be my own propitiation. To absorb my own wrong with regret, to pay it down with disciplines, to make myself feel bad enough that the debt would seem covered. It is exhausting and it never works, because the conscience knows the price and knows I cannot meet it. The gospel is not that God lowered the price. The gospel is that he paid it. And that is why "we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1) — not a truce, not a probation, but peace, because the wrath was not ignored. It was satisfied.

Which leaves no room for boasting. "Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded" (Romans 3:27). It always is. A gift you could not earn cannot be a thing you brag about. You can only kneel under it.

Just, and the one who justifies.

## Abraham Believed God
*Counted righteous before he lifted a finger*

**Text:** Romans 4:1-25 · **Supporting:** Genesis 15:6 · Genesis 17:10-11 · Psalm 32:1-2 · Romans 10:9

If Paul is going to say that God justifies sinners by faith apart from works, he has a problem, and he knows it. Every Jew in Rome had one name ready as the objection. Abraham. The father of the faithful, the friend of God, the man who left everything and obeyed. Surely Abraham earned it. So Paul does not avoid the strongest case against him. He walks straight to it and makes it his witness.

**The order of the words in Genesis**
"What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God" (Romans 4:1-2). Then Paul does what a careful reader of Scripture does. He goes to the verse and he watches the order of the words. "For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness'" (Romans 4:3). He is quoting Genesis 15:6 exactly: "And he believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness."

Counted. Reckoned. The word is an accounting term — credited to an account, entered in a ledger. Righteousness Abraham did not have was credited to him as though he did. And on what basis? Not works. Faith. "Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness" (Romans 4:4-5). Read that phrase and do not soften it: God "justifies the ungodly." Not the godly. Not the improved. The ungodly, the sinner with nothing to bring, who stops working and simply trusts. That is the only kind of person God justifies, because it is the only kind there is.

**Before the circumcision, before the law**
Now Paul plays his decisive card, and it is a matter of chronology. When was Abraham counted righteous? "How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before" (Romans 4:10). Genesis 15 is faith counted as righteousness. Circumcision does not come until Genesis 17 — "Every male among you shall be circumcised... and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you" (Genesis 17:10-11). Years apart. The righteousness was credited while Abraham was still uncircumcised, still indistinguishable from the Gentiles, a man with nothing but a promise and a God he trusted.

Why does the order matter so much? "The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well" (Romans 4:11). If Abraham had been justified by the mark, only the marked could be his children. But he was justified before the mark, by faith, so that everyone who believes — Jew or Gentile, inside the law or outside it — belongs to him. The same logic covers the law itself: "For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be the heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith" (Romans 4:13). Promise, not law. Gift, not wage. And to seal it Paul brings in David, the great sinner, singing the same song from the other side: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven... blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin" (Psalm 32:1-2, quoted Romans 4:7-8). Will not count. The same ledger word. Abraham's righteousness credited in; David's sin not credited against. Two men, two thousand years, one gospel.

**Faith in the God who raises the dead**
What kind of faith was this? Not a vague optimism. A trust in a specific God doing a specific impossible thing. "In hope he believed against hope... He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb" (Romans 4:18-19). His body dead, her womb dead, and God promising life out of both. Abraham believed "in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist" (Romans 4:17). That is the faith that justifies — trust in the God who creates out of nothing and raises out of death.

And Paul will not let it stay in the past. "But the words 'it was counted to him' were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification" (Romans 4:23-25). The same God. The same kind of faith. Abraham trusted God to bring life from a dead womb. We trust God who brought life from a sealed tomb. Paul says the same thing to the Roman church plainly: "if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved" (Romans 10:9).

I need this more than I want to admit, because I am a worker by instinct and a believer only by grace. My reflex is to bring God my résumé, to come with the ledger of things done, to be the one who works and collects his due. And Paul keeps taking the ledger out of my hands and saying: not the one who works. The one who believes. The God who justifies is not impressed by my body of work; he raises the dead, and the only thing I can bring to a resurrection is the deadness that needs it. My standing was credited to me, like Abraham's, before I had done one thing to deserve it and apart from everything I have done since.

Counted righteous before he worked.

## Peace With God in the Second Adam
*One man undid us, one man remakes us*

**Text:** Romans 5:1-21 · **Supporting:** Genesis 3:17-19 · 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 · Romans 8:1 · John 10:28

Paul has built the case for justification. Now he tells you what it feels like to be a justified man standing on the far side of the verdict. And the first word out of his mouth is peace. Not relief. Not a truce. Peace — the war over, the enmity ended, the accused embraced.

**Peace that holds when everything else shakes**
"Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand" (Romans 5:1-2). We stand in grace. Not visit it. Not hope to reach it. Stand in it, the way you stand on a floor you trust with your whole weight. And because the peace is settled, Paul can do the strangest thing. He can boast in suffering. "We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Romans 5:3-5). A man at peace with God can let suffering do its slow work on him instead of being destroyed by it, because the worst thing that could happen — separation from God — has already been made impossible.

**Love proved at the wrong time**
Then Paul measures the love that bought this peace, and he measures it by its timing. "For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6). And again, in case we drifted past it: "but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). While. Not after we cleaned up. Not once we had begun to seek him. While we were still in revolt, still suppressing the truth, still handing ourselves over to the appetites of chapter one — at that moment, the wrong moment, the unflattering moment, Christ died.

This is the death of every notion that God waited for us to become loveable. "One will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die" (Romans 5:7). The best human love rises to meet something worthy. God's love came down to the unworthy. He did not love us because we were good. He loved us, and that is why we will be made good. Get the order wrong and you spend your life trying to earn what was already given to you at your worst.

And this is the quiet rot at the center of so much religion — the assumption, never spoken but always operating, that God's affection tracks our performance. That on the good weeks he draws near and on the bad weeks he withdraws, so that the whole spiritual life becomes a campaign to stay in his good graces. Romans 5 burns that down. The love was proved at the worst possible moment, on the worst possible people, before a single improvement was made. If he loved you while you were still a sinner, his enemy, in active revolt — then your bad week cannot lose what your good week never earned. The cross is not God responding to our progress. It is God acting against our ruin while the ruin was total.

**Two men, two humanities**
Then Paul stands back and shows you the whole of human history as the tale of two men. "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). One man — Adam. In the garden God had said, "cursed is the ground because of you... by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground... for you are dust, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:17-19). One act of disobedience, and the whole race went down into condemnation and death. We did not each independently invent sin. We were born into a fallen family, downstream of a representative who failed.

But a representative can be replaced. That is the gospel hidden in the comparison. "For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many" (Romans 5:15). As Adam stood for his people and brought them down, Christ stands for his people and brings them up. "For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19). Paul says it the same way to Corinth: "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:21-22). Two men, two humanities, and your whole future hangs on which one represents you.

And then the line that should ruin every accountant's view of God. "Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more" (Romans 5:20). Where sin increased. Not where sin was modest. Grace does not merely match our sin. It overwhelms it, outruns it, abounds beyond it, so that the deepest pit of guilt is still shallower than the mercy poured over it.

I confess I do not live as a man at peace. I live, too often, as a man still negotiating the treaty, still bringing God evidence that I am improving, still bracing for the wrath as though it were not already spent at Calvary. And Paul keeps telling me the war is over. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). The representative held. The obedience of the second Adam is reckoned to me as surely as the disobedience of the first was. Jesus said of his own, "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand" (John 10:28). That is the peace. Not that I have finally become loveable, but that I am held by one whose grip does not depend on my performance — held by the obedience of another, at peace because of a man I am not.

Where sin increased, grace abounded more.

## Dead to Sin, Alive to God
*Grace is not a permit*

**Text:** Romans 6:1-23 · **Supporting:** Colossians 2:12 · Romans 8:13 · Galatians 2:20 · 1 Peter 2:24

Paul has just said it — where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. And he knows exactly what the carnal heart does with a sentence like that. It hears permission. If my sin only makes grace look better, then why not sin more and let grace shine? Paul names the objection in the first breath of chapter six, because it is the objection every cheap version of Christianity has lived on ever since.

**By no means — you died**
"What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:1-2). His answer is not a new rule. It is a fact about who you now are. You died. Something happened to you in Christ that makes the question itself absurd, the way it would be absurd to ask a freed slave why he does not report for work in the morning.

"Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:3-4). This is the heart of it. When Christ died, you died — united to him, joined to his death the way a branch is joined to the vine. And when he rose, you rose. Paul says the same to Colossae: "having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith" (Colossians 2:12). Your old self, the man you were in Adam, was crucified with Christ. "We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin" (Romans 6:6). The chain is broken. Sin is no longer your master. It may still be your tempter, but it is not your owner.

**Consider it true, then act on it**
So what do you do with a death and a resurrection you cannot feel? You reckon it. "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" (Romans 6:11). Consider — the same accounting word from chapter four, reckon it true, count it as fact. The Christian life begins by believing what God says is already so about you, before you feel a shred of it. You are dead to sin. Now think of yourself that way when the temptation comes, because the temptation is lying about who you are.

And then — only then, after the indicative, never before it — the command. "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions. Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life" (Romans 6:12-13). Present yourselves. Hand the body over to God deliberately, the same body that in chapter one was handed over to its appetites. There are only two masters and you will serve one. "Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey?" (Romans 6:16). There is no neutral. There is no unowned self. The question is never freedom from all masters. The question is which master.

**Free for righteousness, not free from God**
"But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart... and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness" (Romans 6:17-18). This is the freedom the gospel gives — not autonomy, which was Adam's lie, but a change of ownership. You were freed from the master who paid in death so you could be bound to the master who gives life.

This is the answer to the whole modern dream of the unowned self, the sovereign individual who belongs to no one and bows to nothing. Paul says that self has never existed. Every person is presenting his members to a master — to the appetite, the ambition, the fear, the resentment that has quietly taken the throne. The man who congratulates himself on serving no one is usually the most thoroughly enslaved, because his master wears no chains he can see. The gospel does not offer to make you your own. It offers a better Lord, one who does not pay his servants in death. And the test of which master you serve is not what you claim but what you obey when no one is watching — "you are slaves of the one whom you obey" (Romans 6:16). The body keeps the honest record. It always reports for duty to its real owner. And Paul ends with the wage and the gift side by side, the cleanest summary of the whole letter in a single verse. "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23). Sin pays. It always pays, and the currency is death. God does not pay; he gives, and the gift is life.

I have to confess that I have used grace exactly the way Paul forbids. Not crudely — I would never have said why not sin so grace abounds. I said it quietly, in the back of my heart, every time I let a sin stand because I knew forgiveness was cheap and near. That is the abuse Paul is killing. And the cure he hands me is not more willpower. It is the truth that I am already dead to that thing, joined to Christ, no longer its slave, and that to go back to it is to act like a corpse pretending it still owes its old master a day's labor. Paul put his own life in those terms: "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). And Peter grounds it where it must be grounded — in the cross: "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness" (1 Peter 2:24). He bore it there so that you could die to it here. The same Spirit that raised him says now: "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13).

You died. Now live like it.

## The War the Law Could Not Win
*The good command that could not make you good*

**Text:** Romans 7:1-25 · **Supporting:** Exodus 20:17 · Psalm 19:7 · Romans 8:3-4 · Matthew 5:6

If grace is the answer and the law could not justify us, the obvious question is whether the law was the villain all along. Whether the commandment itself is the problem, a cruel thing, a trap. Paul reaches the place in his argument where someone is bound to think it, and he refuses the easy slander. He will not blame the law. He will do something far more honest. He will blame us, and acquit the law, and then show you why even a perfect law could never save a broken man.

**The law is holy; the law cannot give life**
"What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet'" (Romans 7:7). He quotes the tenth commandment — "You shall not covet your neighbor's house... or anything that is your neighbor's" (Exodus 20:17). And he tells the truth about what the law did in him. It did not make him good. It told him what good was, and in the telling, it stirred up everything in him that wanted the opposite. "For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness" (Romans 7:8). The fence does not create the trespasser, but it shows him there is a fence, and something in the fallen heart wants to climb it precisely because it is there.

So Paul renders his verdict on the law, and it is not condemnation. "So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good" (Romans 7:12). The psalmist sang it: "The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psalm 19:7). The law is not the enemy. The law is a mirror that shows you the dirt, and you do not break the mirror for telling the truth. The problem was never the standard. The problem is the one standing in front of it.

This matters because there are two ways to get the law wrong, and most of us live in one of them. The first is to despise it — to treat the commandments as an old burden the gospel finally lifted, so that grace becomes an excuse to stop caring what God said is good. Paul has already killed that error in chapter six. The second is to trust it — to make law-keeping the engine of our standing with God, to believe that if we just clamp down hard enough on the flesh we can produce the righteousness the commandment demands. Paul kills that one here. The law is good, and the law cannot save, and holding both truths at once is the beginning of spiritual sanity. The commandment that says do not covet is holy. And it has never once stopped a man from coveting. It can light the room. It cannot mend what the light exposes.

**The war every honest believer knows**
Then Paul opens his chest and lets us see the war inside, and it is the most quoted description of the divided heart ever written. "For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" (Romans 7:15). "For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing" (Romans 7:18-19). Every Christian who has ever fought a sin and lost knows this paragraph from the inside. You want the good. You truly want it. And you find a power in you stronger than your wanting, dragging you the other way. "For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive" (Romans 7:22-23). War. Not metaphor. The believer feels two laws pulling against each other in his own body, and the law of God, holy and good, points at the failure but cannot win the fight. It can command the good. It cannot supply the strength to do it.

**The cry, and the answer that is a name**
And the war drives Paul to a cry. Not a strategy. Not a technique. A cry. "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?" (Romans 7:24). Notice he does not ask what will deliver him — what program, what discipline, what fresh resolve. He asks who. The deliverance the law could never give cannot be a thing. It has to be a person. And the answer comes before the question has even settled. "Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (Romans 7:25).

This is the whole point. The law was never able to provide what it required. It could write the demand. It could not write the obedience into the heart. And so God did what the law could not. "For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us" (Romans 8:3-4). What the law could not do, God did in his Son. The righteous requirement we could never meet was met in Christ and then fulfilled in us by his Spirit. The deliverance is not a better effort. It is a better representative and a new power.

I know this chapter because I live this chapter. I have preached holiness on a Sunday and lost the same battle by Tuesday, doing the very thing I hate, wanting the good in my inner being and watching another law win in my members. And the temptation, when that happens, is to reach for the law again — to clench harder, resolve more, build a stricter fence. Paul says the fence was never the cure. The cure is a person and a cry. The Christian life is not the discovery that I have finally become strong. It is the daily return to the only one who can deliver me, the hunger that Jesus promised would be filled: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied" (Matthew 5:6). The cry of chapter seven is not a failure of faith. It is what faith sounds like in a man who is still being saved.

Who will deliver me from this body.

## No Condemnation, No Separation
*The two walls that bound the Christian's whole life*

**Text:** Romans 8:1-39 · **Supporting:** Romans 5:8 · Romans 8:32 · Ephesians 1:13-14 · John 17:24

Chapter eight begins with no condemnation and ends with no separation, and between those two walls stands the entire life of the believer. Everything Paul has argued for seven chapters — the wrath, the verdict, the propitiation, the union with Christ, the war within — comes to rest here, in a chapter that starts with a court acquittal and ends with a love nothing can break.

**No condemnation — and the reason is not you**
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). Now. Not someday, not if you finish well, not after a probation. Now. And the ground is not your improvement; it is your position — in Christ Jesus. The wretched man of chapter seven, still fighting, still failing, is told there is no condemnation hanging over him, because the condemnation already fell on his Savior. "For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do" (Romans 8:3). The verdict is in and it cannot be reopened.

And the same Spirit who frees you from condemnation gives you life and leads you home. "For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (Romans 8:14-15). Adoption. The fatherless taken into the family, given the name, given the standing of a child, taught to call the Holy God Father. "The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ" (Romans 8:16-17). Not servants hoping to be kept. Children who cannot be disowned.

**Everything bent toward glory**
Then Paul widens the lens to the whole groaning creation and the believer's place in it. The sufferings are real — "the sufferings of this present time" (Romans 8:18) — but they are weighed against a glory so heavy they cannot tip the scale. And in the middle of the groaning, the most steadying sentence a suffering Christian owns. "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28). All things. Not all good things. All things — the loss, the diagnosis, the failure, the war within — bent by God toward the good of his children, which Paul immediately defines not as comfort but as Christlikeness: "to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29).

And he traces the chain that holds it, link by unbreakable link. "Those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified" (Romans 8:30). Look at the tense on that last word — glorified, past tense, a thing not yet seen but already so certain in the mind of God that Paul speaks of it as done. The chain has no broken link. No one falls out between the calling and the glory. The God who started it finishes it.

**Nothing — and he means nothing**
Then Paul throws open the courtroom one last time and dares anyone to bring a charge. "What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?" (Romans 8:31-32). Read that argument. The hardest thing God could ever give, he has already given — his own Son, not spared, handed over. If he did the costliest thing while we were still sinners ("God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us," Romans 5:8), every lesser thing is now certain. "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died — more than that, who was raised — who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us" (Romans 8:33-34). The Judge has already acquitted you and the Son is praying for you. The court is empty of accusers.

And so the chapter ends where the whole letter was always going. "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?" (Romans 8:35). He lists the very worst the world can do and then sweeps the whole universe for one thing that could cut the cord. "For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39). Nothing in the list. Nothing left off the list. Nothing.

I have to be honest about how little I believe this on an ordinary day. I live as though my standing were a thing I could lose by Thursday, as though the love were conditioned on the week I am having. And Paul takes the whole anxious project away from me. The love that holds me was not earned by me and so it cannot be lost by me. It rests on the Son who was not spared, sealed by the Spirit who is "the guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians 1:13-14), and aimed at a day Jesus himself prayed for: "Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory" (John 17:24). That is where the chain ends. Not in my grip on God. In his grip on me.

Nothing can separate us from him.

## Has the Word of God Failed
*The mercy that does not run on merit*

**Text:** Romans 9:1-11:36 · **Supporting:** Genesis 25:23 · Exodus 33:19 · Isaiah 10:22 · Romans 11:36

Paul has just said nothing can separate us from the love of God. And immediately a shadow falls across the promise. Because Israel — the people of the promise, the nation that carried the oracles, the family the Messiah came from — Israel has largely refused him. So the question is not academic. It is the whole thing. If God's chosen people can fall away, what is my no separation worth? Has the word of God failed?

**The grief before the argument**
Notice how Paul begins. Not with logic. With tears. "I am speaking the truth in Christ — I am not lying... that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh" (Romans 9:1-3). Before he defends the sovereignty of God, he grieves for the lost. He would trade his own salvation for theirs if he could. Whatever Paul is about to say about election, he is not saying it coldly. He says it on his knees, weeping. Any doctrine of God's sovereignty that does not weep for the lost has stopped being Paul's.

**The word did not fail; it never ran on bloodline**
Then the thesis. "But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel" (Romans 9:6). The promise never attached to mere physical descent. It always ran along a line God chose. And Paul proves it from their own family tree. Isaac, not Ishmael. Jacob, not Esau — and chosen before either was born: "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad — in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Romans 9:11). God had said it to Rebekah while the twins were still in the womb: "the older shall serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). The choice was God's, made before the boys had done a thing, so that it could rest on his calling and not on their record.

And Paul knows exactly how that lands on us. We feel the protest rise. So he voices it, fairly and at full strength. "You will say to me then, 'Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?'" (Romans 9:19). He does not dodge it. He grounds the answer where it has to be grounded — in who God is. "Has the potter no right over the clay?" (Romans 9:21). And he quotes God's own self-revelation to Moses: "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion" (Exodus 33:19, quoted Romans 9:15). Here is the thing we resist with everything in us: mercy that is not owed cannot be demanded. The moment you could require it, it stops being mercy and becomes wages. The whole point of mercy is that it belongs to the giver to give.

**The remnant, the grafting, and the wideness of mercy**
But Paul does not end in hardening. The argument bends toward an astonishing breadth. God has kept a remnant — "so too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace" (Romans 11:5), just as Isaiah foresaw: "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved" (Isaiah 10:22, cited Romans 9:27). And Israel's stumbling was not the end of Israel; it became the door for the world. "Through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles" (Romans 11:11). The Gentiles are wild branches grafted into a cultivated tree, and Paul warns them not to grow proud — "do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20) — because the God who broke off natural branches can graft them in again, and means to. "A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:25-26).

And then Paul cannot argue anymore. He breaks into worship. "Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!" (Romans 11:33). The doctrine of election does not end in a debate. It ends in a doxology. The man who has stared deepest into the sovereignty of God comes out not arguing but adoring.

Notice where Paul stops. He does not stop at a tidy system that resolves every tension. He stops at the edge of what a creature can know and calls it depth, not contradiction. There is a kind of theologian who treats the sovereignty of God as a puzzle to be solved, a position to be defended, a club to be won — and that man has never wept like Paul wept in verse three. And there is another kind who flattens the mystery the other way, who cannot abide a God who hardens and shows mercy as he wills, and so quietly edits the passage until God becomes manageable. Paul does neither. He holds the full weight of it — real human responsibility, real divine freedom — and instead of resolving it he worships at it. "Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?" (Romans 11:34). No one advised God on the rescue of the world. We were not in the room. We are only the rescued.

I have to confess that my instinct toward this whole section is to defend God or to defend my freedom, to take a side and win the argument. And both reflexes miss what Paul is doing. He is not handing me a position to hold against opponents. He is taking my hands off the controls. If mercy ran on merit — on my seeking, my deciding, my doing — then I would have something to boast about, and Romans has spent ten chapters demolishing every last thing I might boast in. The hard comfort here is that my salvation does not finally depend on the strength of my grip but on the freedom of his mercy. The same mercy that humbles me is the only mercy strong enough to hold me, because it never ran on me to begin with. Paul ends the whole towering argument in three small phrases that put me in my place and put God in his: "For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen" (Romans 11:36).

Mercy belongs to God alone.

## Living Sacrifice, Renewed Mind
*What eleven chapters of mercy ask of a body*

**Text:** Romans 12:1-13:14 · **Supporting:** Leviticus 1:9 · Romans 5:8 · 1 John 4:19 · Mark 12:31

For eleven chapters Paul has been pouring out the mercies of God — the wrath answered, the sinner justified, the dead made alive, the elect held, the lost grieved over and grafted in. And then comes one word that turns the whole letter from doctrine to doorstep. Therefore. Everything before it was God's mercy. Everything after it is the only fitting response. And notice the order, because the order is the gospel: the mercy comes first, and always first, and the obedience flows out of it. Never the reverse.

**The altar you climb onto and stay on**
"I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship" (Romans 12:1). By the mercies. Not by threat, not by fear, not to earn anything — Paul has spent eleven chapters proving you cannot earn it. The pull is the mercy itself. And what he asks for is the body. Not a feeling, not an opinion, not an hour on Sunday. The body — the same body that in chapter one was handed over to its appetites, the same members that in chapter six were to be presented to God. Lay it on the altar.

But a living sacrifice. The old sacrifices died — "the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the Lord" (Leviticus 1:9). Paul's twist is that this offering stays alive on the altar, and that is the difficulty of it. A dead sacrifice is offered once. A living one keeps trying to crawl off. To present your body as a living sacrifice is to climb onto the altar every morning and stay there all day, when every nerve in you wants down.

**Stop being pressed into the world's shape**
"Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect" (Romans 12:2). The world has a shape it wants to press you into, and it presses constantly, from the outside in. Paul says the counter-pressure works the other way — from the inside out, through a renewed mind. You are not changed by clenching your behavior. You are changed by a new way of thinking that reshapes the behavior. The renewed mind is not information added. It is the gospel sinking deep enough to retrain what you love and want and reach for by reflex.

And out of that renewed mind comes a love with no pretense in it. "Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good" (Romans 12:9). Then Paul lets the practical commands fall like rain — outdo one another in showing honor, be patient in tribulation, bless those who persecute you, "Repay no one evil for evil... do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Romans 12:17-21). This is what a sacrificed body looks like on a Tuesday. Not heroic. Ordinary. Honoring the annoying brother, blessing the one who wronged you, refusing the small revenge.

And before any of that, the renewed mind does its first work on the self. "For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment" (Romans 12:3). The world's whole project is to inflate the self — to build a brittle case for your own importance and then defend it against every threat. The gospel does the opposite. A man who knows he was justified while ungodly has nothing left to prove and nothing left to protect, and that emptied man is finally free to honor his brother above himself, to weep with those who weep, to associate with the lowly. Sober judgment about the self is not self-hatred; it is the relief of no longer having to be impressive. The living sacrifice has already given the self away. There is nothing left on the altar to defend.

**Owe nothing but love**
And the sacrificed life reaches even into how the Christian sits under authority. "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God" (Romans 13:1). Pay what you owe — taxes, revenue, respect, honor. And then Paul gathers the whole of it into a single debt that is never paid off. "Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law" (Romans 13:8). Every other debt you can clear. This one you carry forever, because love is not a transaction you complete but a current that keeps running. "Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law" (Romans 13:10) — which is only Jesus' second great command spoken back: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Mark 12:31).

I have to admit how often I have reversed Paul's order, and reversing it is the death of joy in the Christian life. I have tried to be a living sacrifice in order to feel that God accepts me, when Paul says present your body because he already has, by the mercies, freely, in Christ. Get it backwards and obedience becomes a frantic attempt to secure a love I am terrified of losing, and a body forced onto an altar by fear will not stay there an hour. Get it right and obedience becomes the overflow of a love already poured out. John named the engine: "We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). And Paul has already shown us the proof of that first love: "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). He was the true living sacrifice — the body offered once for all, that mine could be offered at all. I do not climb the altar to earn his mercy. I climb it because the mercy already came down to find me, and a heart that has truly seen that cannot help but answer with the only thing it has left to give.

Mercy received becomes a body offered.

## Welcome One Another
*The gospel tested at the dinner table*

**Text:** Romans 14:1-15:13 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 11:10 · Romans 5:8 · Philippians 2:3-4 · John 13:34

It is one thing to be justified by faith. It is another to sit at the same table as a brother who is wrong about food. Paul has built the most towering argument in the New Testament, and he ends it not on a doctrine but on a dinner. Because the place the gospel actually gets tested is not the seminar room. It is the room where the strong and the weak have to eat together and would rather not.

**Two real Christians, one disputed table**
In Rome the church had a fault line running through it. Some believers — Paul calls them the weak — still kept the old dietary laws and held certain days as sacred. Others — the strong — knew their freedom in Christ and ate anything. And each despised the other. "As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables" (Romans 14:1-2). Watch carefully what Paul does and does not do. He does not say the issue is meaningless. He has a view; he sides with the strong. But he refuses to let a disputable matter — a thing where Scripture has not bound the conscience — become a wall in the body of Christ. "Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him" (Romans 14:3).

There it is — the deepest reason. God has welcomed him. You are despising a man God has received. You are sitting in judgment on a brother whose Judge has already acquitted him. "Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls" (Romans 14:4).

Mark how carefully Paul handles both sides, because the temptation runs in two directions and he refuses to flatter either. To the strong he says: do not despise. Contempt is the sin of the free man, the one who looks at his more scrupulous brother and feels superior, enlightened, grown-up. To the weak he says: do not judge. Condemnation is the sin of the careful man, the one who looks at his freer brother and sees compromise, laxity, a slide toward worldliness. Each is sure the other is the problem. Each has made a disputable thing into a test of fellowship. And Paul will not let either of them turn a matter of conscience into a doctrine of division, because the moment we do that, we have set ourselves up as lord over a servant who answers to someone else entirely.

**The reckoning that ends the contempt**
Paul lifts both the despiser and the judge into the same courtroom and lets them see the only verdict that finally counts. "Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God" (Romans 14:10). We will all stand there. Not him — all of us. "So then each of us will give an account of himself to God" (Romans 14:12). The cure for contempt is the coming reckoning. When you remember that you will answer to God for yourself, you lose your appetite for answering on his behalf for someone else.

So love sets the limits of liberty. "Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother" (Romans 14:13). The strong are right about the meat and still called to lay the freedom down when it would wound. "If your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (Romans 14:15). Read that last phrase. The one for whom Christ died. You would spend over a menu what Christ purchased with his blood. "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Romans 14:17). My liberty is real, but it is not the kingdom, and I will surrender it before I will damage a soul Christ bled for.

**The pattern is a person**
And then Paul gives the whole thing its center, and the center is Christ. "We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up. For Christ did not please himself" (Romans 15:1-3). There is the model. Christ did not please himself. He bore with us. He welcomed the failing, the weak, the wrong — and we were not merely wrong about meat, we were his enemies. "While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). So Paul lands the command on the cross. "Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God" (Romans 15:7). That is the measure. Not welcome the ones who agree with you. Welcome one another the way Christ welcomed you — and he welcomed you while you were still his enemy, at infinite cost, before you had a single thing right.

I have to confess how often I have done the very opposite from the very seat where I should know better. I have despised the brother whose convictions are tighter than mine and called it maturity. I have judged the brother whose freedom is wider than mine and called it conviction. Both are contempt, and contempt for a man God has welcomed is contempt aimed past him at God. Paul will not let me build a wall the cross tore down. Christ welcomed me at my worst, over the deepest of all disputable matters — whether I would have him at all — and he welcomed me anyway. Jesus made it the new commandment: "A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved one another, you also are to love one another" (John 13:34). And the welcome was always meant to be this wide — Isaiah saw it long ago: "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope" (Isaiah 11:10, quoted Romans 15:12). A table with room for the strong and the weak, the Jew and the Gentile, the one who eats and the one who abstains — every kind of welcomed sinner, seated together, because one Host welcomed them all.

Welcome each other as Christ welcomed you.
